Council Briefing

Assembled from the ATNI Energy Task Forces site.

Nothing is in the packet yet. Start from one of the packets above, or tick plates and checklists in the list.

What this packet says

  1. Counted to the screen, an hour of chat is about 15 Wh, streamed video 14, and agentic coding 211 AI page; 16 sourced figures, 5 partly verified.
  2. Amazon spent 132 billion dollars against 123 billion of cash and securities; Apple spent 9 against 137 AI page; 14 sourced figures.
  3. An hour of chat and an hour of video overlap: about 15 and 14 Wh, 12 Wh of each your own screen and router AI page; 46 sourced figures, 17 partly verified.
  4. A text prompt is seconds to minutes of streaming; an agent session is hours on every yardstick AI page; 19 sourced figures, 8 partly verified.
  5. An average weekly ChatGPT user's text prompts cost about 1 Wh a day in the data center, an illustration AI page; 20 sourced figures, 5 partly verified.
  6. All of ChatGPT's text messages are a few tenths of a terawatt-hour a year; the buildout adds hundreds AI page; 25 sourced figures, 6 partly verified.
  7. By 2035, BLS projects +34.6 percent for data scientists and -25.5 for data entry keyers AI page; 16 sourced figures.
  8. By 2035, BLS projects +25.1 percent in computing and hosting and -4 in office and administrative support AI page; 8 sourced figures.
  9. Studies disagree, and every row measures a different thing AI page; 21 sourced figures, 5 partly verified.
  10. In nine months, capital spending passed operating cash flow at Amazon: 176 billion dollars against 114 AI page; 46 sourced figures, 1 partly verified.
  11. Google's electricity rose 37 percent in 2025 to 43.6 TWh AI page; 25 sourced figures, 2 partly verified.
  12. For 2026, Amazon guides to about 220 billion dollars and Alphabet to 195 to 205; Apple and NVIDIA give none AI page; 21 sourced figures, 5 partly verified.
  13. Market capitalization on 10/30/2026 ran from about 1,572 billion dollars (Meta) to 5,008 (Apple) AI page; 26 sourced figures, 12 partly verified.
  14. The Council puts data centers and chip fabs at 2,475 aMW in 2030, in a region using 22,000 today Data Centers page; 17 sourced figures, 5 partly verified.
  15. A 125 MW project at a 0.8 load factor would average 100 aMW, 0.45 percent of the region's load today Data Centers page; 7 sourced figures.
  16. EIA's baseline puts data center servers at 105 TWh in 2025 and 178 by 2030 Data Centers page; 8 sourced figures.
  17. LBNL counts 192 TWh for US data centers in 2024 and 649 by 2030 in its reference case Data Centers page; 11 sourced figures.
  18. The IEA counts 485 TWh for the world's data centers in 2025 and about 945 by 2030 in its base case Data Centers page; 8 sourced figures, 1 partly verified.
  19. 15 editions of 18 put 2023 US electricity sales high; 7 editions of 9 put commercial sales low Data Centers page; 44 sourced figures, 7 partly verified.
  20. Power, water, and carbon have agency figures; land, heat, and materials have one or two modeled ones Data Centers page; 22 sourced figures, 7 partly verified.
  21. A 100 MW site's evaporative cooling consumes about 190 to 810 million liters a year on site Data Centers page; 10 sourced figures.
  22. On a consumption basis, operators report 0.27 to 1.15 liters per kWh Data Centers page; 12 sourced figures, 2 partly verified.
  23. The filings read state no land for 41 of the 83 named proposals Data Centers page; 23 sourced figures, 23 partly verified.
  24. Walla Walla County's May to September daytime high averages about 87 F in 2040 to 2059, up from 84 F Data Centers page; 528 sourced figures, 528 partly verified.
  25. A 100 MW site implies about 70 to 200 construction workers at peak and 15 to 35 permanent staff Data Centers page; 31 sourced figures, 14 partly verified.
  26. About 1 Wh of a 188 Wh streamed hour happens in the data center on one account, 0.6 (0.3 to 3.1) Wh on another Energy and Water Use page; 9 sourced figures.
  27. The forecasts for 2030 disagree: 380 to 790 TWh for the United States in one set of scenarios, 521 to 843 TWh in another Energy and Water Use page; 12 sourced figures, 2 partly verified.
  28. US data centers consumed 66 billion liters on site in 2023, and the power plants serving them nearly 800 billion more Energy and Water Use page; 7 sourced figures, 1 partly verified.
  29. Worldwide use reached 485 TWh in 2025, and the IEA's base case roughly doubles it by 2030 Energy and Water Use page; 7 sourced figures, 1 partly verified.
  30. Hold one boundary at a time: the data center alone, or the whole chain of a streamed hour Energy and Water Use page; 20 sourced figures, 4 partly verified.
  31. Efficiency, solar, and electrification lead 44 Tribes' public plans; no finding concerns offshore wind or marine energy Tribal Energy page; 20 sourced figures, 20 partly verified.
  32. 4 dated deadlines in the catalog through 08/31/2028; 8 more open or forecasted programs carry no date Tribal Energy page; 14 sourced figures, 10 partly verified.

From the Data Centers page

Consent

A checklist for Tribal leaders before any data center proposal, drawn from CRITFC’s water questions, the Yakama Nation’s findings, Cherokee Nation’s task force report, and the Department of Energy’s diligence questionnaires (CRITFC; Yakama Nation; Cherokee Nation; DOE Office of Indian Energy). Items marked “for counsel” are legal questions, not conclusions.

  1. Have citizens been asked, in a survey, town hall, or referendum, and what did they say? Cherokee Nation’s task force collected 1,593 survey responses from citizens before the Principal Chief acted.
  2. Who is the true counterparty and end user: developer, hyperscale operator, or investor? Has the Council seen every non-disclosure agreement, and does any NDA keep officials from speaking with their own people?
  3. Does the proposal reach ceded lands, Treaty-protected places, or cultural sites, and have Treaty and cultural resource staff reviewed it before any inquiry is answered?
  4. Is “no” or “not yet” still an available answer at every stage?

This comparison does not decide a proposal.

Default settings, sources checked 11/05/2026.

From the Data Centers page

Land

A checklist for Tribal leaders before any data center proposal, drawn from CRITFC’s water questions, the Yakama Nation’s findings, Cherokee Nation’s task force report, and the Department of Energy’s diligence questionnaires (CRITFC; Yakama Nation; Cherokee Nation; DOE Office of Indian Energy). Items marked “for counsel” are legal questions, not conclusions.

  1. What is the land status (trust, allotment, fee), and does the Tribe have approved HEARTH Act leasing regulations? For counsel: does the existing leasing code cover a data center and its generation, or is an amendment, a Tribal Energy Resource Agreement, or a Section 17 entity the better vehicle (BIA, HEARTH Act)?
  2. What lease term is requested, and what happens to the land and improvements when it ends?
  3. Which law governs the facility, Tribal environmental, zoning, and permitting codes or state and local ones, and who enforces it?

This comparison does not decide a proposal.

Default settings, sources checked 11/05/2026.

From the Data Centers page

Water

A checklist for Tribal leaders before any data center proposal, drawn from CRITFC’s water questions, the Yakama Nation’s findings, Cherokee Nation’s task force report, and the Department of Energy’s diligence questionnaires (CRITFC; Yakama Nation; Cherokee Nation; DOE Office of Indian Energy). Items marked “for counsel” are legal questions, not conclusions.

  1. What is the cooling design, and how much water does it withdraw and consume across all operating phases? Is closed-loop or air cooling a binding term, not a promise? Try the cooling instrument.
  2. What is the source (surface, aquifer, or municipal), and what is its hydrological connection to salmon-bearing streams?
  3. Under drought and low-flow conditions, could withdrawals push streams below what fish passage, spawning, or rearing need? Has cumulative withdrawal with existing agricultural, municipal, and industrial users been assessed?
  4. Have Tribal water rights and instream flow needs been specifically accounted for? For counsel: where a reserved or Treaty water right is unquantified, what must be filed, and where, to keep a new large user from being permitted ahead of it (DOJ, Federal Reserved Water Rights)?
  5. What is discharged, at what temperature, with what chemicals, into what receiving water, and are there Tribal fishing sites or cold-water refuges downstream?

This comparison does not decide a proposal.

Default settings, sources checked 11/05/2026.

From the Data Centers page

Power

A checklist for Tribal leaders before any data center proposal, drawn from CRITFC’s water questions, the Yakama Nation’s findings, Cherokee Nation’s task force report, and the Department of Energy’s diligence questionnaires (CRITFC; Yakama Nation; Cherokee Nation; DOE Office of Indian Energy). Items marked “for counsel” are legal questions, not conclusions.

  1. How many megawatts at full load, and who generates it? Is on-site generation fossil-fueled, and what are the air permit and emissions commitments, including backup generators?
  2. Will the load add pressure on the hydropower system during peak or emergency conditions, when fish protections are suspended?
  3. Who pays for transmission, substation, and fiber upgrades, and who owns them afterward?

This comparison does not decide a proposal.

Default settings, sources checked 11/05/2026.

From the Data Centers page

Rates

A checklist for Tribal leaders before any data center proposal, drawn from CRITFC’s water questions, the Yakama Nation’s findings, Cherokee Nation’s task force report, and the Department of Energy’s diligence questionnaires (CRITFC; Yakama Nation; Cherokee Nation; DOE Office of Indian Energy). Items marked “for counsel” are legal questions, not conclusions.

  1. Is there a large-load tariff that assigns the facility’s full cost of service, with minimum billing, collateral, and exit charges? Oregon’s POWER Act, Grant PUD’s terms, and NorthWestern’s filing are reference points (Oregon PUC; Grant PUD; NorthWestern Energy).
  2. Will Tribal members’ electricity bills rise, and has a Tribal utility or the serving utility modeled it before signing?

This comparison does not decide a proposal.

Default settings, sources checked 11/05/2026.

From the Data Centers page

Jobs

A checklist for Tribal leaders before any data center proposal, drawn from CRITFC’s water questions, the Yakama Nation’s findings, Cherokee Nation’s task force report, and the Department of Energy’s diligence questionnaires (CRITFC; Yakama Nation; Cherokee Nation; DOE Office of Indian Energy). Items marked “for counsel” are legal questions, not conclusions.

  1. What are the realistic permanent jobs and wages? The Department of Energy puts permanent staffing at “a few to a few dozen” per facility (DOE FAQ). Try the jobs instrument.
  2. Are local hiring, apprenticeship, and training commitments written into the agreement, with a public dashboard and audit rights?

This comparison does not decide a proposal.

Default settings, sources checked 11/05/2026.

From the Data Centers page

Data

A checklist for Tribal leaders before any data center proposal, drawn from CRITFC’s water questions, the Yakama Nation’s findings, Cherokee Nation’s task force report, and the Department of Energy’s diligence questionnaires (CRITFC; Yakama Nation; Cherokee Nation; DOE Office of Indian Energy). Items marked “for counsel” are legal questions, not conclusions.

  1. If Tribal data will be hosted, under what terms? Which TSDF tier does each dataset carry, and does the contract bar the operator from using, training on, or retaining it (Resolution #2026-034, PDF)?
  2. Whose law governs the data, and in whose courts?

This comparison does not decide a proposal.

Default settings, sources checked 11/05/2026.

From the Data Centers page

Exit Terms

A checklist for Tribal leaders before any data center proposal, drawn from CRITFC’s water questions, the Yakama Nation’s findings, Cherokee Nation’s task force report, and the Department of Energy’s diligence questionnaires (CRITFC; Yakama Nation; Cherokee Nation; DOE Office of Indian Energy). Items marked “for counsel” are legal questions, not conclusions.

  1. What happens if demand for AI computing contracts: minimum payments regardless of occupancy, parent guarantees, decommissioning bonds, and reversion of improvements?
  2. For counsel: what is the narrowest waiver of sovereign immunity a Tribe or Tribal entity can grant (forum, remedies, assets reachable, term), and could an arbitration or governing-law clause operate as a broader waiver than intended?
  3. Has independent legal, financial, and technical counsel, not paid by the developer, reviewed the full deal?

This comparison does not decide a proposal.

Default settings, sources checked 11/05/2026.

From the AI page

Before a Tribe adopts an AI tool

Drawn from ATNI resolutions and the public evidence above, and offered to member Tribes as a starting point, not a standard; each Tribe sets its own.

  1. Who reviews what the tool produces, and who has the power to stop its use?
  2. Can Tribal staff read, change, and shut off the tool?
  3. At which tier is the data the tool will touch, and does that tier allow it?
  4. Which work stays with staff, so the skill stays with them too?
  5. Against which trusted source will each output be checked?
  6. Will language or cultural material go into the tool, and who has consented?
  7. Where does the computing run, and under whose law?
  8. What evidence, beyond the vendor's claims, shows that the tool works?
  9. Which relationships or teaching would the tool stand in for?

This comparison does not decide a proposal.

Default settings, sources checked 11/05/2026.

From the Energy and Water Use page

Developer: load and workload

Tribal Nations are sovereign governments, and each will decide for itself whether a data center fits its homelands, waters, and relatives. The figures above support three requests in any first meeting: a number in the units that matter (megawatts, gallons, acres), the method behind it, and a commitment to keep reporting it. The first meeting does not need to wait for better public data. Ask the developer for each item in the disclosure table above, for this site, and get the answers in writing.

  1. What are the nameplate capacity in megawatts, the expected average load in megawatt-hours a year, and the phases by year?
  2. What share of the load will be AI training, AI inference, general cloud, or cryptocurrency mining, and will the racks be conventional (about 8 to 11 kW) or AI-class (about 120 kW)?

This comparison does not decide a proposal.

Default settings, sources checked 11/05/2026.

From the Energy and Water Use page

Developer: water

Tribal Nations are sovereign governments, and each will decide for itself whether a data center fits its homelands, waters, and relatives. The figures above support three requests in any first meeting: a number in the units that matter (megawatts, gallons, acres), the method behind it, and a commitment to keep reporting it. The first meeting does not need to wait for better public data. Ask the developer for each item in the disclosure table above, for this site, and get the answers in writing.

  1. Which cooling design will be used, and what are annual water withdrawn, consumed, and discharged in gallons, with peak-day demand? Which definition of water usage effectiveness is used (withdrawal or consumption, IT energy or total energy)?
  2. What is the source (surface, groundwater, or municipal; potable or not), what volume does the current permit allow, and how is it connected to nearby salmon-bearing streams? CRITFC's question list asks the same.
  3. What is the discharge's volume, temperature, and chemistry, where does it go, and can the receiving treatment plant handle it in drought, in low-flow years, and if the project grows?

This comparison does not decide a proposal.

Default settings, sources checked 11/05/2026.

From the Energy and Water Use page

Developer: power and flexibility

Tribal Nations are sovereign governments, and each will decide for itself whether a data center fits its homelands, waters, and relatives. The figures above support three requests in any first meeting: a number in the units that matter (megawatts, gallons, acres), the method behind it, and a commitment to keep reporting it. The first meeting does not need to wait for better public data. Ask the developer for each item in the disclosure table above, for this site, and get the answers in writing.

  1. Will the facility draw from the grid, generate its own power, or both, with what fuel, and for how many hours a year will backup generators run?
  2. Can the facility reduce load on request? A test in Arizona cut a data center's peak-hour use by about a quarter (reported by the Council).

This comparison does not decide a proposal.

Default settings, sources checked 11/05/2026.

Developer: disclosure, hardware, and land

Tribal Nations are sovereign governments, and each will decide for itself whether a data center fits its homelands, waters, and relatives. The figures above support three requests in any first meeting: a number in the units that matter (megawatts, gallons, acres), the method behind it, and a commitment to keep reporting it. The first meeting does not need to wait for better public data. Ask the developer for each item in the disclosure table above, for this site, and get the answers in writing.

  1. Will the developer publish electricity and water by site each year, verified independently, and keep doing so after a sale, a lease, or a change of tenant?

From the Energy and Water Use page

Utility

Tribal Nations are sovereign governments, and each will decide for itself whether a data center fits its homelands, waters, and relatives. The figures above support three requests in any first meeting: a number in the units that matter (megawatts, gallons, acres), the method behind it, and a commitment to keep reporting it. The first meeting does not need to wait for better public data. Ask the developer for each item in the disclosure table above, for this site, and get the answers in writing.

  1. What load does the utility forecast for the project (average megawatts and load factor), and how does it compare with the Council's data center and chip fab input of 1,512.8 to 4,988.7 average megawatts in 2030?
  2. Where does the power come from in a normal year and in a low-water year, and which convention does the utility use for hydropower's indirect water and emissions?
  3. Where is the project in the interconnection queue, and how does the utility treat speculative requests?
  4. Who pays for new generation, transmission, and substations, and which minimum-payment and exit terms protect other customers?
  5. Will the utility consult the Tribal government before it commits, rather than after?

This comparison does not decide a proposal.

Counsel

Tribal Nations are sovereign governments, and each will decide for itself whether a data center fits its homelands, waters, and relatives. The figures above support three requests in any first meeting: a number in the units that matter (megawatts, gallons, acres), the method behind it, and a commitment to keep reporting it. The first meeting does not need to wait for better public data. Ask the developer for each item in the disclosure table above, for this site, and get the answers in writing.
